body:
The same man who founded DeLand founded this town too

Lake Helen's origin story runs directly through DeLand's. The area was first settled around 1858 by James H. Prevatt and known as the Prevatt Settlement. When Judge Prevatt died in 1883, Henry DeLand, the same founder who gave the neighboring city of DeLand its name and its ambitions, bought 340 acres of the Prevatt estate and kept buying until he had roughly 1,000 acres. In 1884 he surveyed and mapped the new town, and named both the town and its lake after his daughter, Helen Parce DeLand. Lake Helen incorporated in the summer of 1888. For a new agent, that shared founder is a genuinely useful fact: Lake Helen and DeLand aren't just neighboring towns, they were built as part of the same founder's vision, at nearly the same time.

A real Victorian winter resort, not just a farm town

Early in 1884 a sawmill started up, and on Thanksgiving eve that same year, DeLand opened the Harlan House to attract winter visitors from the north. G.C. Courtright, a merchant from Scranton, Pennsylvania, later owned the Harlan Hotel, and M.L. Granville owned the Granville House. Between the two hotels, Lake Helen became a real destination for New Englanders escaping northern winters, not just an agricultural outpost. That resort-town identity, genuine hospitality infrastructure built specifically for seasonal visitors, is part of why Lake Helen's surviving architecture reads as distinctly Victorian rather than purely rural Florida vernacular.

The railroad, a growth surge, then the freeze that emptied it back out

The railroad reached Lake Helen in 1887, and the town grew quickly in the years that followed, with new homes built every season as northern visitors and settlers arrived. That growth surge is part of why the town has real, substantial Victorian building stock instead of just a handful of scattered structures: for roughly seven years, Lake Helen was genuinely booming. Then the winter of 1894-95 brought Florida's catastrophic “big freeze.” Most of Lake Helen's citrus trees were destroyed, and with them, the livelihood of many of the town's founding families. Many left afterward. It's the same freeze that reshaped DeLand and towns across Central Florida, and Lake Helen's small size meant the loss hit proportionally harder here than in larger neighboring towns with more diversified local economies. Two of the town's historic churches, Lake Helen First Congregational Church (1887) and Blake Baptist Church (1894), date from opposite ends of that same short boom-to-bust window, real physical bookends to the story.

Seventy-one buildings that survived to become a real historic district

What makes Lake Helen genuinely distinct today is how much of that Victorian-era town actually survived. The Lake Helen Historic District, designated on September 16, 1993, covers about 350 acres and contains 71 protected buildings, a real mix of Victorian, Mediterranean Revival, and Craftsman styles standing side by side, physical evidence of how the town grew and changed across several decades rather than in one uniform building boom. For an agent, a historic district this size in a town this small is a genuine differentiator: buyers looking for real architectural character, not a recreated version of it, have very few other options this size in the county.

The spiritualist camp next door, and a real Lake Helen connection

Lake Helen sits immediately next to Cassadaga, home to the Cassadaga Spiritualist Camp, one of the oldest active religious communities of its kind in the country. The connection to Lake Helen itself is real and documented: George P. Colby, the camp's founder, lived in Lake Helen from 1875 to 1925 and formed the Southern Cassadaga Spiritualist Camp Meeting Association in December 1894, the same year as the great freeze. Cassadaga is its own unincorporated community, not part of Lake Helen, but the two are close enough, and connected enough through Colby's own history, that buyers researching one often find the other. An agent working this market should know the real relationship rather than conflating the two or leaving a buyer confused about which address they're actually looking at.

A town that has genuinely resisted modernization, on purpose

Hopkins Hall, built in 1897 as a community center and library, still stands today, restored, alongside the town's historic churches and its 71-building district. With a population of roughly 3,000, Lake Helen has stayed small by choice as much as by circumstance: there isn't a single stoplight in the entire city, and the tree-lined residential streets and light traffic are a deliberate part of the town's identity, not an oversight. For an agent, that's worth saying plainly to a buyer: Lake Helen isn't an undiscovered version of a bigger town waiting to catch up, it's a small town that has actively chosen to stay one.

faq.a: Henry DeLand, the same founder behind the city of DeLand, bought the land in 1883 and named the town and its lake after his daughter, Helen Parce DeLand. Lake Helen incorporated in 1888.

faq.q: What is the Lake Helen Historic District?
faq.a: Designated in 1993, the Lake Helen Historic District covers about 350 acres and protects 71 buildings in Victorian, Mediterranean Revival, and Craftsman styles, one of the best-preserved historic districts of its size in Volusia County.

faq.q: Is Lake Helen the same as Cassadaga?
faq.a: No. Cassadaga, home to the Cassadaga Spiritualist Camp, is its own unincorporated community next to Lake Helen. The two are closely connected historically: the camp's founder, George Colby, lived in Lake Helen from 1875 to 1925, but they are separate places.

faq.q: Why does Lake Helen have so many historic buildings?
faq.a: Lake Helen was built as a genuine Victorian-era winter resort in the 1880s with real hotels drawing visitors from the northeast, and a large share of that original building stock survived, leading to its 71-building historic district today.
